answer.sourceLine: Bezos said these lines on stage at the AWS re:Invent Day 2 fireside chat with Werner Vogels, in a recording uploaded by Amazon Web Services on 29 November 2012 — Quote Investigator transcribes both questions from that video ↗. He had already made the same point in print in “The Institutional Yes,” his October 2007 Harvard Business Review interview ↗, where he asked it about “the next five to ten years.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 2012 re:Invent Day 2: Fireside Chat with Jeff Bezos & Werner Vogels
Video uploaded by Amazon Web Services, 29 November 2012
“The Institutional Yes,” Harvard Business Review, October 2007
Spoken remarks, on video — transcribed by Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: I very frequently get the question: ‘What’s gonna change in the next 10 years?’ … I almost never get the question: ‘What’s not going to change in the next 10 years?’ And I submit to you that that second question is actually the more important of the two…
trail: Summer 1998 — Rubbermaid chairman and CEO Wolfgang R. Schmitt uses the same inversion in a Marketing Management roundtable, per Quote Investigator ↗. A precursor to the thought, not to Bezos’s sentences.

October 2007 — the idea first appears in print under Bezos’s name in “The Institutional Yes,” his Harvard Business Review interview with Julia Kirby and Thomas A. Stewart ↗. QI quotes it ↗ with “the next five to ten years” rather than ten.
24 December 2007 and 7 June 2011 — QI documents ↗ a looser version in The Daily Telegraph and another at Amazon’s shareholders meeting, showing Bezos working the same point repeatedly.
29 November 2012 — the familiar wording is spoken at the AWS re:Invent fireside chat with Werner Vogels, in the video Amazon Web Services published ↗. This is the version that circulates.
source.excerptNote: This is Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗, ellipses and all. The gap between the two questions is QI’s, and the spoken “gonna” is usually written out as “going to” when the line is quoted.

author.name: Jeff Bezos
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Who was Jeff Bezos?
author.bio: Jeffrey Preston Bezos was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico on 12 January 1964 and founded Amazon in mid-1994, running it as chief executive until 5 July 2021, when he became executive chairman. He also founded the spaceflight company Blue Origin in September 2000 and bought The Washington Post on 5 August 2013. The “what won’t change” framing is one of his most durable rhetorical habits — he returned to it in print, at shareholder meetings and on stage over more than a decade.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is sound — this really is Bezos, and there is video. What circulates wrongly is the packaging: the wording is tidier than the transcript, the numbers differ from the print original, and the idea has an older ancestor Bezos is not usually asked about.

items.why: Quote Investigator's transcription ↗ places an ellipsis between the two questions, so the popular text runs together lines that were separated by intervening speech. QI also renders the first as “What's gonna change” — the spoken contraction that circulating versions tidy up.

In the October 2007 Harvard Business Review interview QI quotes ↗, Bezos asks about “the next five to ten years” in both halves. The matched ten-year framing is the later spoken form, not the print original.

QI documents the chairman and CEO of Rubbermaid using the same inversion in a Summer 1998 Marketing Management roundtable: “Everybody's looking forward, thinking about what's going to change, and I thought I'd talk about what's not going to change with regard to new product innovation” ↗. This is a precursor to the thought, not the source of Bezos's sentences.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator's verdict is unambiguous: “Jeff Bezos deserves credit for the quotation which appeared in the 2007 HBR interview. Bezos has revisited this theme several times over the years” ↗ — and the familiar ten-year wording is one of those revisits, spoken at re:Invent in 2012.

context.heading: Why the second question was the point
lead: Bezos was not being cute. He used the inversion as a strategy argument: predictions about change are unreliable, so a business should be built on the handful of customer desires that will still be true in a decade. In the October 2007 Harvard Business Review interview where the idea first appears in print, he put the conclusion plainly — “It helps to base your strategy on things that won’t change” ↗.

He kept returning to it. Quote Investigator documents the framing in a Daily Telegraph interview on 24 December 2007, again at Amazon’s shareholders meeting on 7 June 2011, and then in the 2012 re:Invent form that became the version everyone quotes.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted between 2007 and 2012
detailsBody: The 2007 print original asks about “the next five to ten years” in both halves. The Telegraph version from December 2007 uses a flatter phrasing: “I often get the question ‘In the next 10 years, what is going to change?’ But I rarely get the question ‘What is not going to change?’”
The crisp parallel construction — “very frequently” against “almost never,” ten years against ten years — belongs to the spoken 2012 re:Invent delivery. That is the version that spread.
context.pull: It helps to base your strategy on things that won’t change.

Harvard Business Review published an October 2007 interview with Jeff Bezos titled 'The Institutional Yes' by Julia Kirby and Thomas A. Stewart. (Page metadata confirms title, authors and issue date; the article body is paywalled, so the quoted passage itself rests on Quote Investigator's citation.)

Jeff Bezos was born 12 January 1964 in Albuquerque, New Mexico; founded Amazon in mid-1994; served as CEO until 5 July 2021, then became executive chairman; founded Blue Origin in September 2000; bought The Washington Post on 5 August 2013.
Wikiquote's Jeff Bezos page carries sourced quotations and gives his birth date as 12 January 1964, but does NOT contain this ten-years quotation in any section.
